description: Grab a broom by the end of the handle and start levering. Your wrist lever number exposes the wrist tendons, the last link in every grip and press. Learn how these small cables transfer all your forearm power, the five mistakes that leave them weak, and the lever protocol that forges them.

beats.text: ONE BROOM. HELD AT THE END.
THE LAST LINK IN THE CHAIN

scenes.narration: Grab a broom or a mop and hold it by the very end of the handle, one hand, arm straight out in front of you. The broom head points up like a flag. Now, keeping your elbow straight and your forearm still, use only your wrist to lower the broom slowly toward horizontal, then lever it back up. That is one rep. Count how many slow, controlled reps you get before the broom starts wobbling and your wrist has to cheat. That number is your WRIST LEVER TEST. It looks like a party trick. It is actually a direct reading of the tendons that cross your wrist, the final link between your forearm muscles and everything you will ever grip, press, or hold. Write the number down. At the end I will tell you what it means.

scenes.label: SLOW LEVER REPS PER SIDE
scenes.narration: Here is the line. TEN slow lever reps on each side means your wrist tendons transfer forearm power without buckling. Under five is where nearly everyone starts, because nobody trains this link on purpose. Over twelve, you own the kind of wrists that make heavy grips feel light and push-ups feel solid, and wrists like that are built, never inherited.
scenes.sub: under 5: weak link - 5 to 9: building - over 12: wired wrists

scenes.narration: Look at your wrist and notice what is missing: muscle. The wrist itself is almost pure hardware, bone, ligament, and TENDONS, more than nine major cables threading through tunnels on their way from the forearm to the hand. The muscles that move your wrist and fingers live up in the forearm. Every unit of their force has to travel through these cables, around the corner of the wrist, to reach your hand. That makes the wrist the chain's most honest link. A strong forearm with soft wrist tendons is a powerful engine on a slipping clutch. Force arrives late, the wrist bends when it should stay straight, and power leaks into wobble. The lever test measures the clutch directly, because a broom held at the end is a long lever, and a long lever multiplies every weakness in the cable that resists it. The wrist also has a direction problem most people never train. Cables that lift the hand backward are usually weaker than the ones that pull it down, because gripping dominates daily life. A complete wrist is strong in both directions, and the lever test, done both ways, shows you the imbalance honestly.

Why does such a light broom feel so heavy? Leverage. Holding the end of a long handle turns a small weight into a serious torque at the wrist, and torque is the language tendons listen to. The lowering half of the rep matters most. As the broom descends slowly, the wrist tendons lengthen under tension, and that loaded lengthening is the strongest known signal for tendon remodeling. Rush the lowering and you throw the signal away. This is the same principle behind heel drops for the Achilles and slow stand-ups for the knee, applied to the smallest cables in the chain. Different joint, same law: the tendon builds on the way down, under control, over weeks. Master the descent of a broom and you have learned the master key of tendon training itself.

Follow the chain and you will find this link inside everything. Your dead hang is only as strong as the wrist that keeps your hand closed around the bar. Your push-up leaks power every time the wrist collapses back instead of stacking straight over the hand. Even your pull-up quietly depends on wrist tendons holding the grip angle while the big muscles pull. One hundred percent of the force your forearm produces crosses this one small bridge. That is why lifters with impressive forearms sometimes have unimpressive grips, and why small, unglamorous lever work upgrades exercises it never touches. Strengthen the bridge and traffic flows across your whole upper body. Ignore it and every road ends at the same weak toll booth.

Your edge here is recovery. The wrist tendons are small, the loads are modest, and the work takes two minutes, which means you can train this link almost daily while bigger muscles are still recovering from their sessions. Frequency is the skinny guy's superpower across this whole channel, but nowhere is it more unfair than at the wrist. The heavy guy will do his forearm day once a week, if he remembers. You can lever a broom every morning while the kettle boils, stacking hundreds of quality loading cycles a month. Tendons keep the receipts, and your receipt book fills up faster. It also explains a mystery from the dead hang episode. When your grip fails on the bar, it is often the wrist angle that went first, quietly bending until the fingers had no leverage left. Fix the wrist and the hang gets longer without the fingers changing at all.
Lever with me. Broom at the end of the handle, thirty seconds of slow reps, fifteen of rest, four rounds, switching sides each round. The way down is the workout. Go.

Now the five mistakes destroying your wrist tendons. Mistake one: training grip only. Squeezing builds the forearm engine while the wrist cables, the transmission, get nothing. Mistake two: dropping the lowering. If the broom falls instead of descending, you deleted the half of the rep that builds tendon. Mistake three: bending the elbow or swinging the arm, which lets bigger muscles steal the work. Mistake four: starting with the heaviest object in the house. Leverage is load, and a long broom is already heavy where it counts. Mistake five: training one direction only, lifting the broom but never levering it the other way, so half the cables stay soft. The fix takes two minutes a day: slow levers, both directions, both sides, elbow locked straight. And if one spot on your wrist stays sore for weeks, or your fingers start tingling, see a professional. Small cables still deserve a real diagnosis. Chalk the broom handle at the grip point. Same hand position every session means the lever length never changes, and your numbers stay honest month after month.

scenes.label: RETEST THE LEVER
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under FIVE: the link is weak, which is normal, and weak links are the best news in training because they improve fastest. Five to nine: the transmission is building, and daily levers will push you quickly. Over TEN: your wrist transfers power like a solid bar, and everything upstream of it gets to show off. Use your weaker side as the official number, always. Retest in thirty days with the same broom, the same grip at the very end. Put today's number in the comments. Just the number. The thread will tell the story.
scenes.sub: same broom, grip at the very end, weaker side counts

scenes.narration: Your grip was never the whole story. The bridge it crosses was. Give your wrist cables thirty days of slow levers and bring me the new number. Subscribe, because next we go to the biggest spring in your body, the Achilles, and most guys are training it backwards. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 wrist tendon training Mistakes That Are Destroying Your wrist tendons
